title: The falls that went under
teaches: The Columbia turned into a stair of reservoirs, and Celilo Falls drowned in 1957
summary: **Celilo Falls was a fishing place for about ten thousand years.** The whole Columbia poured over a basalt ledge there, and people fished it with dip nets from wooden platforms until 1957.
**A falls is a difference in level.** What matters is how far the water above stands over the water below, and anything that raises the water below shrinks the falls.
**Backwater drowned Celilo every June.** In the snowmelt flood the river piled up behind the narrows downstream, and the water below the falls rose faster than the water above.
**A reservoir is nearly flat.** Water stands at the dam's height and reaches upstream until the river's own bed climbs above it, which is how a dam 15 km away drowned the falls on 10 March 1957.
**The Columbia is now a stair of lakes.** Eleven dams between Canada and the tide turn its 400 m drop into steps, and above the tide only the Hanford Reach still runs free.
**Most of the dams pass the river straight through.** Their lakes are long but hold only days of flow; the storage dams, Grand Coulee and the dams in Canada, can hold back weeks of it.
**Storage flattens the year.** Water held back from the June snowmelt is let out in autumn and winter, so the river now runs lower in June and higher in winter than it did.
**Grand Coulee stopped the salmon.** Built too tall for fish ladders, it ended the runs to the upper Columbia and Canada.

blocks.text: A few kilometres upstream of the town of The Dalles, Oregon, the Columbia used to fall over a ledge of black basalt. It was all of the river at once: the water gathered from British Columbia, Montana, Idaho and most of Washington and Oregon, dropping into a jumble of channels and eddies cut in the rock. The people who lived beside it called the falls Wyam. Most maps called them Celilo Falls.

Salmon heading upriver to spawn had to get past the falls, and they gathered in the eddies below them to rest before they tried. Fishers stood on wooden platforms built out over the white water and swept long-handled dip nets through those eddies. Excavations at Five Mile Rapids, a short way downstream, found salmon bones in layers about ten thousand years old, and the falls were a fishing place and a trading place for the peoples of the river through all the centuries since.[^treaty]

In 1855 the Yakama, the Warm Springs, the Umatilla and the Nez Perce nations signed treaties with the United States that kept, in writing, their right to take fish "at all usual and accustomed places". Celilo was the best known of those places. A century later it was still fished the same way, from platforms, with dip nets, by families who had fished it for generations.

On 10 March 1957 the Army Corps of Engineers closed the gates of The Dalles Dam, about 15 km downstream. Crowds gathered on the banks to watch, many of them families who fished there. Through the day the water below the falls rose to meet the water above, the noise of the falls faded, and by evening Celilo was under a lake.

Two things about this are puzzling. The dam stood out of sight around a bend, 15 km away. And the falls had a habit of nearly disappearing every summer long before any dam was built. The second puzzle is the place to start.

parts.title: A falls that drowned every June

blocks.text: Lesson 2 drew a river's year as a hydrograph, its discharge against time. The Columbia's year at The Dalles had one great swell in it. Through autumn and winter the river ran low, because most of the basin's winter precipitation fell as snow on the Rockies and the Cascades and stayed there. In April the snow began to melt, and by June the river carried five or six times its winter flow. The snowmelt flood of late spring is called the **freshet**.

At low water, in autumn, the river dropped several metres over the ledge at Celilo, around 6 m (20 feet) by most accounts. In the freshet the drop shrank, and in a big year it vanished for weeks. The reason was downstream. Below the falls the whole river had to squeeze through the Long Narrows and Five Mile Rapids, slots of basalt far narrower than the river's usual width, the rapids that gave The Dalles its name. A narrow slot passes a small flow easily, but a big flow has to pile up behind it until it is deep enough to push through. So in June the water below the falls rose faster than the water above them.

blocks.caption: Celilo Falls at low water, in the June flood and since 1957. A falls is the difference between the level above and the level below: raise the water below and the falls shrinks, whatever the river does above.

blocks.text: A falls is a difference in level: how far the surface above the ledge stands over the surface below it, whatever the height above the sea or the amount of water going over. Water raised by an obstruction downstream is called **backwater**,[^backwater] and backwater from the narrows drowned Celilo for part of every year. A dam raises backwater too, and keeps it there all year.

The Columbia falls about 400 m (1,300 feet) between the Canadian border and the sea. Water falling that far carries a great deal of energy, and from the 1930s the Corps, the Bureau of Reclamation and public utilities built dams to turn the fall into electricity. Each dam holds the river up at its face, and its lake reaches back upstream. A lake's surface is nearly flat, so the raised water stands at about the dam's height until the riverbed climbs above it. The Dalles Dam held the river some 25 m (80 feet) higher at its face, and its lake, Lake Celilo, reached back almost 40 km, well past the falls.

Put enough dams in a row and each lake reaches back to the foot of the next dam. The river becomes a stair: flat treads of still water, and the whole drop taken in steps at the dams, where it turns the turbines.[^power]

blocks.caption: The Columbia from the sea to the Canadian border, as the dams went in. Heights are rounded full-pool levels, and the river between dam sites is drawn as a straight slope, so only Celilo shows as a step; heights are stretched about 1,400 times against distances.
blocks.task: Guess, then play the years to 1975

blocks.text: Grand Coulee, finished in 1942, is the tallest step, about 100 m from its lake down to the river below, and it is still the largest power station in the United States. It was built with no way for salmon to pass, because no fish ladder could climb that high.[^ladders] The salmon runs to the upper Columbia and into Canada ended there. Its lake, Lake Roosevelt, runs about 240 km back to the border, and as it filled it drowned Kettle Falls, another great fishing place of the upper river.[^kettle]

By 1968, when John Day Dam filled the last gap below the Snake, the treads met almost everywhere. Above the tide, the only stretch of the Columbia in the United States still running as a river is the Hanford Reach, about 80 km between Priest Rapids Dam and the head of the lake behind McNary. The dams on the Snake and in Canada are not drawn here; they are steps on the same stair.

parts.title: What a dam does to the year

blocks.text: Most of the dams on the stair hardly change how much water goes down the river. Bonneville, The Dalles, John Day and McNary are **run-of-the-river** dams: their lakes are long but shallow for the flow they carry, holding only days of the river's water, so what comes in at the top goes out through the turbines at about the same rate. They change the river's levels and its speed, and they drowned its falls and rapids, but not its year.

A **storage** dam is different. Grand Coulee, the three dams Canada built in the 1960s and 1970s, and tall dams on tributaries in Montana and Idaho have deep lakes that can be drawn down by tens of metres and filled again. Together they hold back water in spring and let it out later in the year. Before you move the slider, think about what that has to do to the hydrograph at The Dalles.

blocks.caption: A typical year at The Dalles, before the dams (a model rounded from monthly means of the old record) and with water held back in spring and let out in autumn and winter. Water held back is shaded blue; water let out later, the colour of the dams.
blocks.task: Guess, then hold back about what the dams hold back today

blocks.text: Every cubic metre held back in June has to come out some time, and it comes out when the river is low. The storage lakes are drawn down through autumn and winter, when the Northwest uses the most electricity, and they are lowest in early spring, which leaves room to catch the next freshet. So the regulated river runs lower in June and higher in winter than the river it replaced. All the reservoirs together could hold back about a third of a year's flow, but in an ordinary year they move less than half of that, because some room is kept empty for floods and some water is saved for dry years, for power and for fish.

The flattened year matters to salmon too. Young salmon heading to sea used to ride the freshet down a fast river; now they cross a string of slow lakes, and part of each spring's flow is let out over the dams' spillways to help them. What happens to the fish themselves belongs to another course. Lesson C2 takes the same storage from the other side: what it does to a flood.

Celilo Village, on the bank above where the falls were, is still home to a small community, and a salmon feast is still held there each spring. The government paid the treaty tribes for the loss of the fishery in the 1950s. Treaty fishing goes on along the river from platforms, boats and nets at other sites the tribes still use.

The falls themselves are under still water, not destroyed: the basalt ledge is down there, under Lake Celilo. If The Dalles Dam were ever taken down, the river would fall over it again, as the Elwha began to run through its old canyon in lesson 4 once its dams came out.

blocks.caption: Six questions on Celilo and the dams
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Long before any dam, Celilo Falls nearly vanished in a big June flood. Which explanation is best?
choices: The water below the falls, backed up behind narrow rapids downstream, rose faster than the water above
Snowmelt carried so much gravel that it filled the pool below the ledge until the river ran level
Spring winds blowing upriver piled the water against the ledge from below for weeks
items.why: A falls is the difference between the level above and the level below. In the freshet the river piled up behind the Long Narrows and Five Mile Rapids, raising the water below Celilo until the step almost disappeared.

items.ask: The Dalles Dam stood about 15 km downstream of Celilo Falls, yet its lake covered them within hours. Why?
choices: A reservoir's surface is nearly flat, so the water stands near the dam's height until the riverbed upstream rises above it
The dam slowed the river so much that sand built up over the falls as soon as the gates closed
Water forced into the ground by the dam came up under the falls and flooded them from below
items.why: The dam held the river about 25 m higher at its face. Still water lies level, so that height reached back almost 40 km, well past the falls.

items.ask: What do storage reservoirs on the Columbia do to the river's year at The Dalles?
choices: Cut the June snowmelt peak and raise the winter flow with the water they let out
Raise the June peak, because the full lakes spill over their dams in the snowmelt
Lower the flow in every month, because the lakes keep back a share of the water
items.why: Water held back in spring is let out in autumn and winter, when the river is low and electricity is most needed. The volume is the same; only its timing changes.

items.ask: Bonneville and The Dalles are run-of-the-river dams. What does that mean for the river below them?
choices: Their lakes hold only days of flow, so water leaves about as fast as it arrives and the river's year hardly changes
Their turbines pass more water than the river brings, so they lower the river below them all year
They store the whole snowmelt each spring and release it at a steady rate all year
items.why: A run-of-the-river dam raises the level and slows the water, but its lake is too small to shift water from one season to another. That takes the storage dams upstream.

items.ask: About how much of the Columbia in the United States, above the reach of the tide, still runs free of a reservoir?
choices: Less than a tenth, mostly the Hanford Reach below Priest Rapids
About half, mostly between the mouth of the Snake and Grand Coulee
About a quarter, mostly in the canyon above Grand Coulee
items.why: Eleven dams turn the river into a stair of lakes, each reaching to the foot of the next. Only about 80 km of the Hanford Reach still runs as a river.

items.ask: Why did Grand Coulee end the salmon runs to the upper Columbia when Bonneville did not?
choices: It was far too tall for a fish ladder and was built with no way for salmon to pass
Its lake was too warm for adult salmon swimming through it in summer
It was built upstream of every stream where the upper river's salmon spawned
items.why: Bonneville was built with fish ladders in 1938. Grand Coulee, about 100 m from lake to river, had none, and the runs above it ended.

treaty.title: Trade at the falls
treaty.text: Fish caught at Celilo were dried and pounded and traded far up and down the river and across the plateau, and the falls drew people from a great distance in the fishing season. Lewis and Clark passed the falls in October 1805 and wrote about the crowds of fishers and the stacks of dried fish.

backwater.title: Backwater
backwater.text: Anything that slows a river from downstream, a narrows, a dam, a high tide at the mouth, or a bigger river at a junction, makes the water stand higher upstream of it. Hydrologists call the raised water backwater and its slope the backwater curve. It is why a gauge's height can rise with no extra water coming down.

power.title: Height and flow make power
power.text: The power in falling water is its weight per second times the height it falls: density × g × flow × drop. Grand Coulee's flow of about 3,000 m³/s falling about 100 m gives 1,000 × 9.8 × 3,000 × 100 ≈ 3 billion watts, a few large power stations' worth, from one dam. The same flow through a 25 m step gives a quarter of that.

ladders.title: Fish ladders
ladders.text: A fish ladder is a staircase of pools, each a little higher than the last, with water running down it so salmon can swim and leap up one pool at a time. Bonneville was built with ladders in 1938, and visitors can watch salmon pass windows beside them. A ladder for a step of 100 m would have been many kilometres long, and none was built at Grand Coulee.

kettle.title: Kettle Falls
kettle.text: Kettle Falls, near the town of the same name in northeastern Washington, was the great fishing place of the upper Columbia. It went under Lake Roosevelt in 1940, while Grand Coulee was still being finished, and people of the upper river held a gathering at the falls that summer to mark the loss, remembered as the Ceremony of Tears.
